newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese hostages savor taste of home in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Japanese hostages savor taste of home in Peru.

text.p: Tension may prevail within the walls of the captured Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, but a touch of delicate home cooking seems to have eased the ordeal for hostages and even some of their captors.
"Japanese food allows variation to meals, and a taste of home was a pleasant surprise for the Japanese hostages," Japanese Red Cross spokesman Akira Nakata told Reuters.
"It also acts as a psychological boost," he added.

Captives inside the residence have relied on food delivered by the Red Cross since Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas stormed a lavish cocktail party there on Dec 17, taking hundreds of VIP guests hostage.
Red Cross officials have been sending Japanese "bento" meals -- which typically consist of rice and assorted dishes of meat, fish, and vegetables -- to the besieged compound since Christmas Eve.

"Japanese hostages released on Wednesday said they really appreciated the traditional meals. They also said Peruvians (hostages) were enjoying it too," said Katsuyuki Tanaka, spokesman for the Japanese diplomatic task force monitoring the hostage crisis in Lima.
For New Year's Eve, Japanese officials decided to treat the ill-fated guests and host Ambassador Morihisa Aoki to a festive touch, in addition to meals prepared by local Japanese restaurants.
"The Red Cross, the (Japanese) foreign ministry and the task force agreed to send a variety of Japanese instant noodles to the hostages," Tanaka said.

One of the four Japanese businessmen released by rebels on Wednesday said he ate a bowl of instant noodles on the evening of Dec 31 as if it were "toshi-koshi soba", traditional noodles eaten on New Year's Eve in Japan, Tanaka added.
Rare cuisine such as this was apparently not only popular with the hostages.
Tokyo's Yomiuri Shimbun daily newspaper quoted one former hostage earlier this week saying that a guerrilla who sampled a "bento" meal out of curiosity looked pleased and told him it tasted good.
The rebels still held 74 hostages on Thursday -- including about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
